reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / corneal dystrophy literature
clinicalPearls: A dystrophy of the corneal endothelium and Descemet membrane, usually inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern
It is characterised by vesicular, band-like or diffuse lesions at the level of Descemet membrane
Many patients are asymptomatic and diagnosed incidentally, with a generally mild course
The endothelial cells acquire epithelial-like characteristics and can migrate abnormally
It may be associated with iridocorneal adhesions, corectopia and, in some, raised intraocular pressure or glaucoma
Most cases need only monitoring, with corneal transplantation reserved for the minority developing significant oedema
reference.pathophysiology: In posterior polymorphous corneal dystrophy the corneal endothelial cells behave abnormally, taking on epithelial-like features with the capacity to proliferate and migrate across the posterior cornea and, at times, onto the anterior chamber angle and iris. This aberrant tissue produces the characteristic vesicular and band lesions of Descemet membrane and can form adhesions that distort the iris and impair aqueous outflow, causing glaucoma in a subset. Endothelial dysfunction can occasionally progress to corneal oedema.
additionalDifferentials: Descemet membrane changes from other cause
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination and specular or confocal microscopy of the endothelium
Assessment of the anterior chamber angle for adhesions
Intraocular pressure measurement and glaucoma assessment
Family history and genetic evaluation in selected cases
redFlags: Raised intraocular pressure or glaucomatous damage
Progressive corneal oedema and visual loss
Features overlapping with ICE syndrome (usually unilateral, non-hereditary)
reference.prognosis: Most cases are mild and stable with a good prognosis; a minority develop glaucoma or corneal decompensation requiring specific treatment or transplantation.
pitfalls: Confusing it with the typically unilateral, acquired ICE syndrome
Attributing corneal oedema to another cause
Missing the autosomal dominant inheritance and need to examine relatives
management: Manage most patients with periodic observation alone, given the frequently mild and stable course
Perform specular or confocal microscopy and monitor endothelial function for early signs of decompensation
Measure intraocular pressure and treat associated glaucoma with pressure-lowering drops, escalating to surgery when medical control is inadequate
Reserve endothelial keratoplasty, or penetrating keratoplasty, for the minority who develop significant corneal oedema
Offer genetic counselling and family examination given the autosomal dominant inheritance
